examples.title: IEEE 14-bus, with machines and controls
examples.summary: The IEEE 14-bus system with a round-rotor machine, an exciter and a governor on each generator: the usual first case for a power flow, a fault study and the eigenvalue analysis.

citations.text: IEEE 14 Bus Test Case, Power Systems Test Case Archive, University of Washington, Department of Electrical Engineering, https://labs.ece.uw.edu/pstca/pf14/pg_tca14bus.htm (accessed 2026-11-17).

ANDES, andes/cases/ieee14/README.md, release 2.0.0: the power flow data of ieee14.raw is by J. Conto and the dynamic data by H. Cui, both written for ANDES (https://github.com/CURENT/andes/blob/v2.0.0/andes/cases/ieee14/README.md, accessed 2026-11-17).

licence.attribution: ANDES asks that research or consulting that uses it cite its paper, which is among the citations of this case (ANDES README, section Citing ANDES).

caveats: The dynamic data (round-rotor machines, a TGOV1 governor on each, an EXST1 exciter on one machine and an ESST3A on each of the other four) was written for ANDES by H. Cui, according to the ANDES cases README, and is not published by the IEEE.

This is not the IEEE 14-bus case as the University of Washington archive distributes it. The line and transformer reactances, the line charging and the shunt at bus 9 are the archive's. The rest was changed in the PSS/E version prepared by J. Conto: the loads at buses 3, 4, 6 and 14 (bus 3 takes 50 MW and 25 MVAr where the archive has 94.2 MW and 19.0 MVAr), a 15 MVAr shunt at bus 14, the dispatch (generators at buses 2, 3, 6 and 8 deliver 40, 40, 30 and 35 MW, where the archive has power at buses 1 and 2 only), the voltage set-points (1.03 pu at buses 1, 2, 6 and 8 and 1.01 at bus 3, where the archive has 1.060, 1.045, 1.010, 1.070 and 1.090), the reactive limits, and the ratio of the four transformers (0.99677 on each, where the archive has 0.978, 0.969, 0.932 and none).

The power flow solution therefore differs from the one the archive stores, by up to 0.06 pu in voltage and 11.8 degrees in angle (bus 8). Do not compare results of this file with published IEEE 14-bus results.
No event is built in. The fault used for the verification is added through the API: a three-phase fault at bus 9 from 1.0 s to 1.1 s.

verification.summary: Compared with independent references: the power flow (bus voltages, angles, losses and the slack's power) agrees with pandapower's solution of the same network to 6e-9 pu and 8.5e-7 degrees. TENSA's power flow was also run on the archive's own data (MATPOWER's case14, which ANDES ships) and reproduces the solution the archive stores to 1.3e-3 pu and 0.017 degrees, which is the precision the archive stores it in (server/tests/integration/test_example_archive_solution.py). That checks the solver, not this file, whose data differ from the archive's. Checks of TENSA against its own linearisation: the undisturbed 10 s run stays at its solution, and the ring-down of a 2% load step has the frequencies and damping ratios of the eigenvalues, within 0.025 Hz and 0.027. Not verified: the fault run and the mode values are TENSA's own earlier output, kept as regression baselines to catch a change. No published result exists for this data.

examples.title: Kundur two-area system, modified by ANDES
examples.summary: Four generators in two areas joined by a weak tie, the standard case for inter-area oscillations, with a round-rotor machine, an exciter and a governor on each generator.

citations.text: P. Kundur, Power System Stability and Control. New York: McGraw-Hill, 1994, ISBN 0-07-035958-X.

licence.attribution: ANDES asks that research or consulting that uses it cite its paper, which is among the citations of this case (ANDES README, section Citing ANDES).

caveats: This is not the system of the book as printed, and its results must not be compared with the book's. The file's own title is "Modified Kundur's two-area test system, distributed with ANDES". It has 10 buses where the book's system has 11, the tie is three parallel lines of 0.22 per unit reactance on 100 MVA, the loads are 1159 MW at bus 7 and 1575 MW at bus 8 with a small net reactive power (-73.5 and -89.9 MVAr), where the book has 967 MW with 100 MVAr and a 200 MVAr capacitor and 1767 MW with 100 MVAr and a 350 MVAr capacitor, and the step-up transformers are 0.012 per unit on 100 MVA where the book's are 0.15 on 900 MVA.

The dispatch and the voltages differ from the book's operating point as well: three generators deliver 700 MW with a set-point of 1.00 pu and the fourth is the slack (about 727 MW in the power flow solution), where the book has 700, 700, 719 and 700 MW and terminal voltages of 1.03, 1.01, 1.03 and 1.01 pu.

The machines match the book's table in their inertia (6.5 s and 6.175 s), reactances (Xd 1.8, Xq 1.7, X'd 0.3, X'q 0.55, X''d and X''q 0.25 per unit) and open-circuit time constants (8, 0.03, 0.4 and 0.05 s), and differ in the leakage reactance (0.06 where the book has 0.2), the armature resistance (0 where the book has 0.0025) and the saturation (none where the book has A = 0.015 and B = 9.6). Each machine has a DC type 2 exciter and a TGOV1 governor, which the book's examples do not.
One event is built into the file: Line_8 is switched out at 2 s.

The eigenvalues the book gives for its system could not be read from any source opened for this entry, and they belong to another network and other exciters in any case, so no published mode is compared.

verification.summary: Compared with an independent reference: the power flow agrees with pandapower's solution of the same network to 2.3e-7 pu and 4.4e-5 degrees. Checks of TENSA against its own linearisation: the undisturbed 10 s run stays at its solution (largest change 3.5e-6), and the ring-down of a 2% load step has the frequencies and damping ratios of the eigenvalues, within 0.007 Hz and 0.005: the inter-area mode at 0.647 Hz with a damping ratio of 0.034 and a local mode at 1.141 Hz. Not verified: the Line_8 trip and the mode values are TENSA's own earlier output, kept as regression baselines to catch a change. No published value is compared, because the file is not the system of the book (see the caveats).

examples.title: WSCC 9-bus, with classical machines
examples.summary: The 3-machine, 9-bus system of Anderson and Fouad with its three machines on the classical model, as in Example 2.6 of the book: the smallest case for a fault, a swing curve and the electromechanical modes of three machines. It has no exciter and no governor.

citations.text: P. M. Anderson and A. A. Fouad, Power System Control and Stability, 2nd ed. Piscataway, NJ: IEEE Press; Hoboken, NJ: Wiley-Interscience, 2003, ISBN 0-471-23862-7, doi:10.1109/9780470545577. The system is the one of Chapter 2 and its Example 2.6.

B. Wang, Y. Liu and K. Sun, "Power System Differential-Algebraic Equations," arXiv:1512.05185, 2015. It prints the classical-model data of this system (H, x'd, the mechanical powers, the internal voltages and the reduced admittance matrix of Example 2.6) that the build of this case is checked against.

H. Cui, F. Li and K. Tomsovic, "Hybrid Symbolic-Numeric Framework for Power System Modeling and Analysis," IEEE Transactions on Power Systems, vol. 36, no. 2, pp. 1373-1384, March 2021, doi:10.1109/TPWRS.2020.3017019.

licence.name: GPL-3.0-or-later
licence.attribution: The file is written by TENSA's scripts/build_wscc9.py and is distributed with TENSA under its licence. The numbers in it are those of the book in the first citation, which is the work to cite for the system.

modifications: The file is written by scripts/build_wscc9.py from the data of the book, not copied from ANDES: the network and the loads are the book's, and the three machines are added as classical models (GENCLS) with the book's inertia constants and transient reactances on the 100 MVA base, no damping and no armature resistance
The power flow solution is stored in the file as the initial state, rounded to six places, as the ANDES example cases do
The transformers are lines with a reactance and the nominal ratio (the book gives a reactance only), flagged as transformers
No fault or other event is built in
caveats: ANDES ships a file of the same network, wscc9/wscc9.xlsx, with no machines. It is not this system: its reactances of lines 4-5, 6-9 and 7-8 (0.068, 0.1738 and 0.0576 per unit) are not the book's (0.085, 0.170 and 0.072), and its power flow differs (the angle of bus 3 is 5.14 degrees against the book's 4.66). Results from the two files must not be compared.

Classical model: constant voltage behind the transient reactance, constant mechanical power, loads as constant impedances and no damping. Its modes lie on the imaginary axis (a damping ratio of 0) and a swing after a fault does not die out.

To run the book's fault, add it in the app: a three-phase fault at bus 7 from 1.0 s to 1.0833 s (5 cycles at 60 Hz) and a trip of line 5-7 (Line_2) at 1.0833 s. With the default step the faster mode swings 1.6 percent slow (the trapezoidal rule's lag, 0.034 Hz at 2.1 Hz); a step of 1/120 s reproduces a continuous solution to a fraction of a degree.

The inertia constants and reactances are per unit on 100 MVA, as the book tabulates them, so each machine is rated at 100 MVA here; the book's machine ratings (247.5, 192 and 128 MVA) are not in the file.

A workspace made by an earlier TENSA holds ANDES's steady-state wscc9.xlsx under this name. Adding this case does not replace that file unless you ask (the force option). The Example cases dialog marks it as a different file and offers to replace it, and tensa examples list says added, differs.

verification.summary: The data was checked against the book: the power flow solution (bus voltages, the generator angles and the slack's power) agrees with the one the book prints, to its printed precision, and the reduced admittance matrix and the initial state of the machines computed from the file agree with those of Example 2.6 as printed by Wang, Liu and Sun, to four decimals (server/tests/unit/test_wscc9_build.py). The power flow agrees with pandapower's solution of the same network to 2e-8 pu. The modes and the book's fault (a three-phase fault at bus 7, cleared after 5 cycles by opening line 5-7) were also computed independently of TENSA and ANDES (Kron reduction, the linearised swing equations, scipy's DOP853 integration), and TENSA agrees: the modes (1.383 and 2.126 Hz, undamped) to 5e-7 Hz, the largest rotor angle spread (85.8 degrees) to 0.004 degrees, the lowest bus voltage to 4e-6 pu and the lowest machine frequency to 1.1e-4 Hz. The undisturbed 10 s run does not move, and the ring-down of a load step has the frequencies of the eigenvalues within 0.034 Hz, which is what the trapezoidal rule's error at TENSA's default step comes to. Not compared: the swing curves of the book's figures, which no source opened gives as numbers, and no published value of the two modes was found. The run is stable and its swings do not die out, as those of an undamped model do not.
